summaries.example: Imagine a class chart with two groups: points and lines. A sentence might say, “For any two different points, there is exactly one line joining them.” Many-sorted logic helps us write this clearly because point variables can only range over points, while line variables can only range over lines. The sorts act like labels that prevent us from mixing up the two kinds of objects.
summaries.summary: Many-sorted logic is a way to describe situations containing different kinds of things. In ordinary first-order logic, variables usually range over one large domain. In many-sorted logic, there is a separate sort, or category, for each kind of object. A variable for points ranges over points; a variable for lines ranges over lines. A structure gives each sort a non-empty domain and explains how relations, functions, and names work. The meaning of a sentence is then determined by asking whether it is true in that structure. The basic rules for “and,” “not,” and “there exists” are much like those in ordinary first-order logic, except that an existence claim specifies a sort. The entry also explains that many-sorted logic can be translated into one-sorted logic, where extra predicates remember which objects belonged to which sorts. It can also serve as a common language for translating other logical systems. Its theorems include important results about proofs and models, while its full decision problem is not always solvable by an algorithm.
key_ideas: Many-sorted logic lets us talk about several kinds of objects in one formal language.
Each sort has its own variables and its own collection, or domain, of objects.
Relations can connect objects from different sorts, such as a line joining two points or an object existing at a time.
Many-sorted first-order logic adds useful labels but remains closely related to ordinary first-order logic.
A many-sorted theory can be translated into one-sorted first-order logic by adding predicates that mark the sorts.
Many-sorted logic can help compare or translate other logics, including some modal and second-order systems.
summaries.why_it_matters: Different subjects often discuss different kinds of objects at the same time. Mathematics may discuss points and lines; a computer program may discuss users, files, and times. Sorts make these differences visible in the language and can make formal descriptions easier to organize. The same framework also helps logicians compare systems and use results about one logic to study another.

important_terms.definition: A kind or category of object, such as points, lines, people, times, or properties.
A formal system for making precise statements and checking whether conclusions follow from them.
A mathematical description with one non-empty collection of objects for each sort, together with relations, functions, and named objects.
A rule that tells us when a sentence is true in a particular structure.

questions_to_think_about: What kinds of objects would you put into separate sorts in a description of a school?
Why might labels help prevent mistakes in a formal language?
Could two different sorts ever contain objects that look similar?
What is the difference between a sentence being written correctly and a sentence being true?
Why might computer scientists want a logic that keeps different kinds of data separate?

summaries.example: Consider a language with two sorts: objects and times. Let E(x,t) mean that object x exists at time t, and let P(t,u) mean that time t precedes time u. A statement about existence through earlier times can quantify over objects and times without treating them as one undifferentiated group. A many-sorted structure supplies one domain for objects and another for times, interprets E as a relation between those domains, and interprets P as a relation on times. The formal sentence is evaluated in that structure using assignments that give each variable an element of the correct sort.
summaries.summary: Many-sorted logic extends first-order logic by replacing one undivided domain with several non-empty domains, called sorts. Its signature records the available relation, function, and constant symbols together with their arities and, in the strict version, the sorts of their arguments. Thus a relation can be required to connect a line with two points, while another can connect an object with a time. Terms and formulas are formed recursively as in first-order logic, but variables and terms must respect these sort restrictions. Semantics follows the familiar model-theoretic pattern: a structure provides domains and interpretations, an assignment gives variables values of matching sorts, and satisfaction determines whether a formula is true. Many-sorted logic retains major first-order metatheorems. A sound and strongly complete calculus can be given, and compactness and Löwenheim-Skolem follow. Its satisfiability problem is nevertheless undecidable in general, although particular fragments can be decidable. The entry presents many-sorted logic as a translation framework. Other systems can be mapped into a many-sorted language through translations of formulas and conversions of structures. Depending on how much correspondence is established, one can transfer results about enumerability, consequence, compactness, or completeness. The system can also be reduced to ordinary one-sorted first-order logic by merging domains and adding unary sort predicates, though many-sorted proofs may remain more economical and conceptually transparent.
key_ideas: A strict relation specifies not only its number of places but also the sorts of its arguments; a liberal relation specifies only its arity.
Terms and variables have sorts, so well-formed formulas must respect the signature's sort information.
Truth is defined in a Tarski-style way: terms receive denotations, and formulas are satisfied under assignments whose values have matching sorts.
Many-sorted first-order logic has sound and strongly complete calculi, as well as compactness and Löwenheim-Skolem results.
It is not a stronger logic than first-order logic in the relevant Lindström sense; its extra organization can be encoded in one-sorted logic.
Translations into many-sorted logic can provide a shared framework for studying modal logic, second-order logic, and related systems.
summaries.why_it_matters: Many-sorted logic separates kinds of entities without abandoning the machinery of first-order model theory. That makes it useful for mathematics, computer science, philosophy, linguistics, and formal semantics, where relations often cross carefully distinguished categories. Its translation role is especially important: instead of treating every logic as isolated, researchers can represent several systems in a common framework and study what semantic and proof-theoretic properties survive the translation.

important_terms.definition: A formal language whose variables are divided into disjoint kinds, with rules specifying which sorts may occur in each relation, function, or constant.
A triple specifying the sorts, the nonlogical symbols, and the sort-and-arity information for those symbols.
A mathematical interpretation of a signature: it supplies non-empty domains for the sorts and interpretations for its symbols.
A method for assigning truth values to formulas relative to a structure and an assignment of values to variables.
A sentence true in every structure of the relevant signature.
The property that every logically implied sentence can be obtained in a proof system.
A result saying that a set of sentences has a model exactly when each finite part has a model.
A translation of a many-sorted language into a one-sorted language by restricting quantifiers with unary predicates for the sorts.

questions_to_think_about: Does adding sorts increase expressive power, or mainly improve organization and clarity?
Why must every sort in a classical many-sorted structure have a non-empty domain?
What information is lost when several sorts are merged into one domain, and how can unary predicates restore it?
Why can a translation preserve useful theorems without making the target logic a replacement for the original language?
What trade-off appears between expressive power and properties such as completeness and compactness?

summaries.example: Suppose you are describing a library system with three sorts: books, readers, and dates. You might want to say, “Every reader borrowed a book on some date.” In a one-sorted language, the variables could range over all objects, so you would need extra statements saying which things are readers, books, or dates. In many-sorted logic, the variable for a reader, the variable for a book, and the variable for a date already come with different labels. A relation such as Borrowed(reader, book, date) can be declared to accept exactly those three sorts.
summaries.summary: Many-sorted logic is a version of first-order logic for settings containing several kinds of objects. Instead of making every variable range over one universe, it assigns variables to sorts, each with its own non-empty domain. A signature specifies the sorts and the symbols of the language, including the permitted sorts and arities of relations and functions. This makes it possible to formalize claims involving, for example, points and lines, individuals and binary relations, or objects and times. The syntax resembles ordinary first-order logic, but quantifiers and terms carry sort information. Its semantics is also familiar: a many-sorted structure supplies domains and interpretations; an assignment gives each variable an element of the correct domain; and satisfaction defines when formulas are true. The source emphasizes that many-sorted logic is not a wholly higher-powered replacement for first-order logic. It can be translated into one-sorted first-order logic by unifying the domains and adding predicates that mark the original sorts. Nevertheless, the many-sorted presentation can be shorter and better suited to applications. The logic has sound and strongly complete proof calculi, along with compactness and Löwenheim-Skolem theorems, but its general satisfiability problem is undecidable. A further role is unification: other systems can be translated into many-sorted logic, with theories and structure conversions designed to preserve their semantics. At different stages, such translations can support results about enumerability, consequence, compactness, and completeness.
key_ideas: Many-sorted logic is designed for statements about several types of objects, not just one general universe.
Sort restrictions can make a formal language clearer, while liberal relations allow arguments from different domains when appropriate.
Its semantics is close to classical first-order semantics: structures interpret symbols, assignments give variables values, and satisfaction determines truth.
Many-sorted logic remains within first-order logic, so it retains central results such as completeness, compactness, and Löwenheim-Skolem.
It can be encoded in one-sorted first-order logic, but this does not mean that the two presentations are equally convenient for every proof or application.
The logic can act as a bridge for studying modal, second-order, and dynamic systems through translations and theories describing the converted structures.
summaries.why_it_matters: The central philosophical and practical issue is how a formal language represents differences among kinds of things. Many-sorted logic builds those differences into the language rather than leaving them to informal explanation. It therefore offers a disciplined way to reason about mixed domains and a shared setting for comparing logical systems. The ability to recover ordinary first-order logic also shows that a useful change in notation and structure need not abandon established logical results.

important_terms.definition: A category of objects in a formal system; variables belonging to that sort range only over its associated domain.
The collection of objects assigned to one sort in a structure; it is required to be non-empty in the classical setting.
A relation, function, or constant together with information about how many arguments it has and which sorts those arguments use.
A mathematical arrangement that interprets a language by providing domains and meanings for its symbols.
A formula that is true in every structure of the appropriate kind.
A proof-system property stating that every conclusion that follows from premises in all models can also be proved from those premises.
A translation that combines all sorts into one domain and uses unary predicates to indicate an object's former sort.
A mapping between logical systems that aims to preserve relevant semantic or proof relationships.

questions_to_think_about: Would sorts change what a language can express, or mainly how safely and clearly it expresses it?
Why might a relation between different domains be more informative than a relation over one undivided domain?
How do validity and consequence differ from simply having a sentence come out true in one model?
Why might a logic with strong general theorems still have an undecidable satisfiability problem?
What could be gained, and what could be lost, by translating a logic into a common target system?
